blocks.text: Aristotle describes this belief as fabulous and explains its origin by the fact that the hyena has, directly beneath the tail, a blind pouch which has the shape of the female genitals [p. 77] and is mistakenly taken for them. In the male the anus lies beneath this blind pouch, and in the female the actual genital opening lies only beneath these two (N. G. 6, 28, 2). Thus that belief arose, and Aristotle in another place (De gener. 3, 6) names Herodorus of Heraclea as the authority for that legend. We should therefore not be surprised if the Talmud embellishes that fable of the hyena's metamorphosis even more prolifically. The mystical number seven plays a principal role in it. The male hyena, it says there, takes on the form of a bat seven years after its birth, again after seven years the form of that bat which is called ערפד, again after seven years that of the stinging nettle, then after an equally long time that of the thornbush, and finally it becomes the evil spirit.

If we strip this strange legend of its embellishment, its ethical teaching is that evil sinks ever deeper and finally reaches the highest degree of depravity. We see from this that the malice and rapacity of the hyena were well known, which we at least wish to note as being correct in terms of natural history. The Talmud is also right in holding it to be tameable, on which one may compare Voigt l. c. 1, p. 279.
The names צבוע and ברדלס are taken from the variegated spotting of the pelt, since the hyena is either striped or spotted.
אפא is probably derived from אף "anger", "malice", since the malice of the hyena is well known; likewise גפרוא seems to be derived from פרן "insolent"; cf. article Parrot on פירוז.

שועל (Aboth 2, 10), חעלא (Joma 43b), pl. שועלים (Sanhedrin 38b). The fox, as is well known, lives at night in burrows it has dug itself or taken from badgers, and by day in the bushes (Voigt l. c. 1. p. 281). The Talmud therefore has a proverb: "The fox does not die in the dust of its burrow", since it mostly stays there and thus remains unharmed by the dust to which it has become accustomed (Nedarim 81b). It also happened that a fox hollowed out a very large gourd and made its nest in it (Ketuboth 111b). That in rich, loose soil the gourd not rarely grows so large that it can reach 2 feet in diameter and weigh about 70 pounds is well known.

Its bite is dangerous and, because of its [p. 78] thin and curved teeth, hardly curable (Aboth 2, 10). It kills young goats and lambs, as well as all kinds of poultry (Chulin 53a and on this Schul. Ar, Jore Dea §. 57, 1), and is especially harmful to vineyards, since grapes are its favourite food (B. Kama 92a*).

Its usefulness consists, besides its pelt, also in this, that the tooth of a living fox prevents a person's sleep (if he keeps it on him), whereas the tooth of a dead one promotes it, for which purposes it was used (Sabbat 67a). Superstition hung a fox's tail between the eyes of a horse, which was supposed to contribute to its well-being (ibid. 53a).
It is not harmful to sown fields, which is why, to describe a futile endeavour, the proverb "He has gained as much as a fox from a ploughed field" is often used in the Talmud (Joma 43b; Nidda 65b).

Its gestation period is 6 months (Bechoroth 8a). It belongs to the small animals (חיה דקה, B. Kama 80a). The fox, since it lacks strength and courage, seeks to obtain its food through cunning, which is why it is said: "Be a tail among lions and not a head among foxes!" (Aboth 4, 15). Others explain this saying to mean that the lion raises its tail vigorously and lashes about with it, while the fox, when caught in its roguery, puts its tail between its legs and runs off, as it were ashamed, as a cowardly thief (see Buxdorf Lex. tal. p. 2619).
When fleeing, in order not to be caught, it does not run straight ahead but makes all possible zigzag leaps (Sota 10a).
Hence of someone whose promising reputation had come to nothing, people exclaimed: "This lion has become a fox!" (B. Kama 117a).

The crafty man sometimes gets further through cunning than the simple man through honesty, but then prudence advises not to have him as an enemy, and hence the proverb: חעלא בעידניה סגיד ליה "When the fox is at the helm, call him politely 'Brother!'" (Megilla 16b, and on this my contribution in the Jüdisches Volksblatt vol. 1, p. 136). Its appearance is also a bad omen to superstition, in which people presumably held the opinion that an undertaking could not succeed if cunning and dishonesty stand to the right, i.e. at its side (Sanhedrin [p. 79] 65b). When running it often turns its head back to look behind it (Midr. Rabba Schemoth fol. 139b).

The fox plays a principal role in the world of fables. Rabbi Meir knew 300 fables about it (ibid. 38b); Rabbi Jochanan b. Sakai is also praised for possessing knowledge of the fox fables (Succa 28a, where Rashi gives information on the origin of the fables); however, only a few of them have been preserved in the Talmud and Midrash, of which we shall give a selection here. I refer here incidentally to a collection
of fables and tales from the animal world of the ancients, which I published in the Jüdisches Volksblatt (vol. 3), from which I here communicate some fables about the fox.
